record.paper_title: The Status of Polycyclic Group-Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: For general polycyclic groups used as platform groups in group-based cryptography, determine bounds on the dimensions of the smallest faithful linear embeddings and determine when faithful linear representations are known and small enough for linear decomposition or linear centralizer attacks to be tractable.

evidence.quote: Moreover, the linear space into which the group is embedded must be of sufficiently small dimension to make the attack tractable.
no such bounds are known for other linear groups, including general polycyclic groups and metabelian groups.
The applicability of the linear centralizer attack to other platform groups is limited to those whose faithful representations are known and whose linear repre- sentations are sufficiently small.
these aspects of polycyclic groups are currently unknown.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A polycyclic group is a group $G$ that admits a subnormal series
$$G = G_0 \triangleright G_1 \triangleright \cdots \triangleright G_n = \{1\}$$
such that each quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. A faithful linear representation of $G$ over a field $k$ is an injective group homomorphism $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_d(k)$; the smallest such $d$ (over a specified family of fields, e.g. $\mathbb{C}$ or finite fields) is called the minimal faithful linear dimension of $G$, denoted $\mu(G)$.

Linear decomposition and linear centralizer attacks against group-based cryptosystems with platform group $G$ run in time polynomial in $\mu(G)$ (and in the size of the field of definition), provided one can effectively compute a faithful representation $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{\mu(G)}(k)$.

Problem. For the class of polycyclic groups (and, more generally, for the subclass of metabelian groups), do the following:

1. Determine explicit upper and lower bounds for $\mu(G)$ in terms of standard invariants of $G$ such as the Hirsch length $h(G)$, the number of generators, the derived length, and the orders of the finite cyclic factors $G_i/G_{i+1}$.

2. Provide a constructive procedure that, given a polycyclic presentation of $G$, either produces a faithful linear representation $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_d(k)$ with $d$ matching the bound in (1), or certifies that no such representation of dimension $\le d$ exists.

3. Characterize those polycyclic groups $G$ for which $\mu(G)$ is small enough (e.g. polynomially bounded in the chosen security parameter) that linear decomposition attacks and linear centralizer attacks against cryptosystems with platform group $G$ become tractable, and conversely identify infinite families of polycyclic groups for which $\mu(G)$ grows superpolynomially, so that such linear attacks are provably infeasible.
artifact.status_search_result: No general bounds on the minimal dimension of faithful linear representations of polycyclic groups (or metabelian groups) appear to be known. Constructive algorithms exist for faithful representations of finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent groups, but the general polycyclic case, together with the cryptanalytic tractability question for linear decomposition / linear centralizer attacks, is still listed as an open direction in subsequent surveys and is not addressed by current results on representation dimension of finite groups.

status_evidence.title: The Status of Polycyclic Group-Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: no such bounds are known for other linear groups, including general polycyclic groups and metabelian groups.
status_evidence.claim: Bounds on faithful linear representation dimensions for polycyclic groups are explicitly stated as unknown.

status_evidence.title: Linear Groups and Computation
status_evidence.snippet: Constructing faithful linear representations of polycyclic-by-finite groups is an important computational problem; an algorithm is known for finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent groups.
status_evidence.claim: Algorithms exist only in restricted subclasses (torsion-free nilpotent), leaving the general polycyclic case open.
